questions.q: Which mechanism explains how magnesium sulfate and lactulose relieve constipation when administered orally?
options: Osmotic retention of water within the intestinal lumen
Direct agonism of enteric muscarinic M3 receptors
Chelation of dietary bile salts in the ileum
questions.explain: Osmotic laxatives act purely through physical osmotic forces, drawing water into the bowel lumen to soften stools and stimulate peristalsis without binding to specific cellular receptors.

open.q: State the physicochemical mechanism by which oral magnesium sulfate and lactulose act as laxatives.

questions.q: How do antacids such as aluminium hydroxide and magnesium trisilicate relieve dyspepsia?
options: By blocking H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells
By direct chemical neutralization of gastric hydrochloric acid
By inhibiting the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump
By stimulating gastrin release from antral G cells
questions.explain: Antacids are weak bases that react chemically with gastric hydrochloric acid to form neutral salts and water, raising intragastric pH without engaging biological receptors.

open.q: Name the direct non-receptor chemical mechanism by which antacids reduce gastric acidity.

questions.q: Which chelating agent acts by forming a stable, water-soluble complex with excess iron in patients with transfusion-induced iron overload?
questions.explain: Deferoxamine specifically chelates free ferric iron (Fe3+) to form ferrioxamine, which is excreted in urine and bile. Dimercaprol chelates arsenic/mercury, and penicillamine chelates copper.

open.q: Name the specific chelating agent used to bind and remove excess iron in acute iron poisoning or chronic iron overload.

questions.q: Which mechanism explains how cholestyramine lowers plasma LDL cholesterol?
options: Binding intestinal bile acids and reducing their reabsorption
questions.explain: Cholestyramine is a non-absorbable anion-exchange resin that sequesters bile acids in the gut, forcing hepatocytes to convert more cholesterol into bile acids and upregulate LDL receptors.

open.q: Describe the non-receptor mechanism by which bile acid sequestrants like cholestyramine lower serum cholesterol.
accept: binds bile acids in the intestine preventing reabsorption
ion-exchange sequestration of bile salts in the gut

questions.q: How does mannitol reduce intracranial pressure in cerebral oedema?
options: It creates an osmotic gradient that draws water from brain tissue into blood
It constricts cerebral arterioles via alpha-1 receptors
questions.explain: Mannitol is a pharmacologically inert, freely filtered sugar alcohol that remains confined to the vascular space and draws interstitial fluid out of oedematous brain tissue via osmosis.

open.q: Explain the physical mechanism by which intravenous mannitol reduces cerebral oedema.
accept: osmotic diuresis and osmotic fluid shift from brain tissue
creates an osmotic gradient across the blood-brain barrier

questions.q: Which enzyme is competitively and reversibly inhibited by neostigmine and physostigmine?
questions.explain: Neostigmine and physostigmine carbamylate the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase, preventing acetylcholine hydrolysis and prolonging cholinergic transmission.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by neostigmine and physostigmine.

questions.q: Which drug acts as an irreversible, non-competitive inhibitor of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) in platelets by acetylating a serine residue?
questions.explain: Aspirin covalently acetylates Ser530 of COX-1; because anucleate platelets cannot synthesize new enzyme, thromboxane A2 synthesis is blocked for the platelet's entire 7 to 10 day lifespan.

open.q: Name the antiplatelet drug that irreversibly acetylates and inhibits cyclooxygenase-1.

questions.q: What is a suicide inhibitor (mechanism-based enzyme inactivator), as exemplified by allopurinol or clavulanic acid?
options: A drug that immediately destroys the host-cell nucleus
A reversible antagonist displaced by high substrate levels
An antibody that precipitates circulating enzymes
A substrate analogue converted by its target enzyme into a reactive inhibitor
questions.explain: In suicide inhibition, the target enzyme catalyzes the conversion of the drug into a reactive product that forms a covalent bond with the enzyme's active site (e.g., allopurinol to oxypurinol on xanthine oxidase).

open.q: Define suicide inhibition in pharmacology and give one clinical drug example.
accept: enzyme converts substrate analogue into reactive inhibitor that covalently binds the active site such as allopurinol or clavulanic acid
mechanism-based irreversible enzyme inactivation exemplified by allopurinol

questions.q: Which drug acts as a false substrate for DOPA decarboxylase in sympathetic nerve terminals, leading to the formation of alpha-methylnoradrenaline?
questions.explain: Methyldopa enters adrenergic neurons and is converted instead of L-DOPA into alpha-methyldopamine and then alpha-methylnoradrenaline, a central alpha-2 agonist used in hypertension in pregnancy.

open.q: Name the antihypertensive drug that acts as a false substrate in the catecholamine synthesis pathway to produce alpha-methylnoradrenaline.

questions.q: How do local anesthetics such as lidocaine and bupivacaine block nerve impulse conduction?
options: Opening voltage-gated K+ channels to hyperpolarise axons
Binding the intracellular Na+ channel pore and blocking sodium influx
questions.explain: Local anesthetics diffuse across the axonal membrane in their uncharged form, re-ionize intracellularly, and block voltage-gated Na+ channels preferentially in their open and inactivated states.

open.q: State the direct ion-channel mechanism by which local anesthetics prevent action potential propagation in nerves.

questions.q: Which class of antidiabetic drugs closes ATP-sensitive potassium (K_ATP) channels on pancreatic beta-cell membranes to trigger insulin exocytosis?
questions.explain: Sulfonylureas bind the SUR1 subunit of beta-cell K_ATP channels, closing them, causing membrane depolarization, opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and stimulating insulin release.

open.q: Name the class of oral hypoglycaemic agents that stimulates insulin secretion by closing pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channels.

questions.q: Which membrane transport protein is directly inhibited by digoxin in cardiac myocytes?
questions.explain: Digoxin inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase, raising intracellular Na+, which reduces the driving force for the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX), increasing intracellular Ca2+ stores and myocardial contractility.

open.q: Identify the sarcolemmal ion pump inhibited by cardiac glycosides such as digoxin.

questions.q: How do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as fluoxetine and sertraline exert their pharmacological action?
options: Blocking presynaptic SERT to increase synaptic serotonin
questions.explain: SSRIs selectively inhibit the Na+/Cl--dependent serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT) on presynaptic nerve endings, enhancing serotonergic neurotransmission.

open.q: Name the presynaptic membrane transporter blocked by SSRIs such as fluoxetine.

questions.q: Which renal tubular transport protein is inhibited by loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide?
options: Na+/Cl- symporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule
Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of Henle
Epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct
SGLT2 cotransporter in the proximal tubule
questions.explain: Loop diuretics inhibit luminal NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, abolishing the corticomedullary osmotic gradient and inducing brisk natriuresis.

open.q: Identify the specific cotransporter inhibited by furosemide in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

questions.q: Which of the following is the fastest-acting receptor superfamily, producing cellular responses within milliseconds upon ligand binding?
questions.explain: Ligand-gated ion channels (such as nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, and NMDA receptors) undergo direct conformational opening of an intrinsic ion pore within milliseconds.

open.q: Name the receptor superfamily that mediates the fastest cellular responses (within milliseconds) via direct ion flux.

questions.q: Which receptor type is the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?
questions.explain: Binding of two acetylcholine molecules to the alpha subunits of the pentameric nicotinic receptor opens a central cation pore permeable mainly to Na+ and K+, causing end-plate depolarization.

open.q: Classify the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor according to its structural receptor superfamily.

questions.q: Binding of benzodiazepines or barbiturates to the GABA-A receptor enhances neuronal inhibition by increasing the conductance of which ion?
questions.explain: The GABA-A receptor is a pentameric ligand-gated Cl- channel; Cl- influx hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic neuron and reduces excitability.

open.q: Which ion flows through the activated GABA-A receptor channel to hyperpolarize neurons?

questions.q: How many transmembrane alpha-helical domains characterize G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)?
questions.explain: GPCRs (metabotropic receptors) are serpentine polypeptides that span the plasma membrane seven times, with an extracellular N-terminus and an intracellular C-terminus coupled to heterotrimeric G-proteins.

open.q: State the number of membrane-spanning domains characteristic of G-protein-coupled receptors.

questions.q: In the resting inactive state of a heterotrimeric G-protein, which guanine nucleotide is bound to the G-alpha subunit?
questions.explain: In the inactive heterotrimer (alpha-beta-gamma), G-alpha binds GDP. Agonist activation of the GPCR promotes exchange of GDP for GTP, dissociating G-alpha-GTP from the beta-gamma dimer.

open.q: Which nucleotide is bound to the alpha subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein in its inactive state?

questions.q: Activation of a Gs-coupled receptor (such as beta-1 or beta-2 adrenoceptors) stimulates which effector enzyme to elevate intracellular cAMP?
questions.explain: Gs-alpha-GTP activates membrane-bound adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cyclic AMP (cAMP), subsequently activating protein kinase A (PKA).

open.q: Name the membrane-bound effector enzyme activated by Gs-coupled receptors.

questions.q: Which intracellular signaling cascade is triggered when an agonist binds to a Gq-coupled receptor (such as alpha-1 adrenoceptors or muscarinic M1/M3 receptors)?
options: Activation of phospholipase C, cleaving PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol (DAG)
Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and opening of GIRK potassium channels
Direct phosphorylation of STAT transcription factors in the nucleus
Stimulation of soluble guanylyl cyclase to raise cGMP
questions.explain: Gq activates phospholipase C-beta, hydrolyzing phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into IP3 (which releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum) and DAG (which activates protein kinase C).

open.q: Name the two second messengers generated when Gq-coupled receptor activation stimulates phospholipase C.

questions.q: What is the specific intracellular role of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) following Gq-coupled receptor activation?
options: Binding IP3 receptors to release stored intracellular Ca2+
Exporting K+ to hyperpolarise the membrane
questions.explain: Water-soluble IP3 diffuses through the cytosol and opens ligand-gated Ca2+ channels on the endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum, causing a rapid spike in cytosolic free Ca2+.

open.q: State the intracellular action of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) in signal transduction.
accept: releases calcium from endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum

questions.q: Which type of G-protein is coupled to muscarinic M2, alpha-2 adrenergic, mu-opioid, and dopamine D2 receptors?
questions.explain: Gi proteins inhibit adenylyl cyclase (lowering cAMP) and their beta-gamma subunits open inwardly rectifying K+ channels (hyperpolarization) while closing voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.

open.q: Which G-protein subtype mediates inhibition of adenylyl cyclase upon activation of M2 muscarinic or alpha-2 adrenergic receptors?

questions.q: How does cholera toxin cause massive secretory diarrhoea at the G-protein signaling level in intestinal epithelial cells?
options: ADP-ribosylating Gs, keeping adenylyl cyclase active
questions.explain: Cholera toxin permanently activates Gs-alpha by preventing GTP hydrolysis, causing continuous cAMP production, CFTR chloride channel opening, and massive water/electrolyte loss.

open.q: Explain the molecular mechanism by which cholera toxin persistently elevates intracellular cAMP in enterocytes.
accept: ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha inhibiting GTPase and keeping adenylyl cyclase active

questions.q: How does pertussis toxin (from Bordetella pertussis) disrupt G-protein-coupled signaling?
options: ADP-ribosylating Gi, preventing inhibition of adenylyl cyclase
Activating Gq to deplete intracellular calcium
questions.explain: Pertussis toxin uncouples Gi from its receptor by ADP-ribosylating Gi-alpha in its GDP-bound form, abolishing Gi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase.

open.q: State the effect of pertussis toxin on heterotrimeric G-proteins.
accept: prevents Gi activation by locking it in GDP-bound state

questions.q: To which receptor superfamily does the insulin receptor belong?
questions.explain: The insulin receptor is a transmembrane heterotetramer with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity that autophosphorylates and phosphorylates insulin receptor substrates (IRS-1/2).

open.q: Classify the insulin receptor according to its transmembrane signaling mechanism.

questions.q: How do nitric oxide (NO) and organic nitrates (such as glyceryl trinitrate) relax vascular smooth muscle?
options: Activating membrane adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP
Activating soluble guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and PKG activity
questions.explain: Nitric oxide binds the haem moiety of cytosolic soluble guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and activating PKG, which lowers cytosolic Ca2+ and activates myosin light-chain phosphatase.

open.q: Name the intracellular enzyme and second messenger mediating vascular smooth muscle relaxation by nitric oxide and nitrates.

questions.q: How does sildenafil potentiate penile erection and lower pulmonary arterial pressure?
options: It directly stimulates nitric oxide synthase in endothelial cells
It blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in corpus cavernosum
It activates adenylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle
It selectively inhibits phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5), preventing the breakdown of cGMP
questions.explain: Sildenafil inhibits PDE5, prolonging the vasodilatory action of nitric oxide-derived cGMP in the corpus cavernosum and pulmonary vasculature.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by sildenafil to prolong cyclic GMP signaling.

questions.q: Where are receptors for glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex steroids, thyroid hormones, and vitamin D located?
options: Inside cells, where they regulate gene transcription
On the cell surface via Gs proteins
questions.explain: Lipophilic hormones diffuse across the plasma membrane to bind intracellular nuclear receptors, which dimerize and bind hormone response elements (HREs) on DNA to alter gene transcription.

open.q: State the cellular location and primary mechanism of action of steroid and thyroid hormone receptors.
accept: intracellular receptors that regulate gene transcription
cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors binding DNA response elements

questions.q: Why do corticosteroids and thyroid hormones exhibit a characteristic lag period of several hours before their full clinical effects appear, even after intravenous administration?
options: They require uptake by Kupffer cells
They alter transcription and require new protein synthesis
They bind almost exclusively to RBC membranes
They must be activated in the kidney
questions.explain: Because nuclear receptors alter mRNA transcription and protein translation, clinical effects develop slowly over hours to days and persist after plasma hormone levels fall.

open.q: Explain why drugs acting on intracellular nuclear receptors (such as hydrocortisone or levothyroxine) have a delayed onset of action.
accept: they require gene transcription and new protein synthesis
time needed for mRNA transcription and protein translation

questions.q: In the resting state before ligand binding, cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors are kept inactive by being bound to which inhibitory chaperone protein complex?
questions.explain: Cortisol binding displaces Hsp90 from the glucocorticoid receptor, unmasking its nuclear localization signal so the hormone-receptor homodimer can translocate into the nucleus.

open.q: Name the chaperone protein released from cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors when a corticosteroid hormone binds.

questions.q: Which signaling pathway is utilized by cytokines such as erythropoietin, interferons, and growth hormone?
questions.explain: Cytokine receptors lack intrinsic kinase domains; ligand-induced dimerization activates associated Janus kinases (JAKs), which phosphorylate STAT proteins that dimerize and enter the nucleus.

open.q: Name the intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling pathway activated by cytokine receptors such as erythropoietin and interferons.

questions.q: In receptor pharmacology, how is 'affinity' distinguished from 'intrinsic activity' (efficacy)?
options: Affinity is receptor binding; intrinsic activity is receptor activation and response
Affinity is maximal effect; intrinsic activity is dose for half-binding
Affinity is measured in hours; intrinsic activity in litres
questions.explain: Both agonists and antagonists possess affinity for the receptor, but only agonists possess intrinsic activity (efficacy > 0) to stabilize the active receptor conformation.

open.q: Distinguish between affinity and intrinsic activity (efficacy) in drug-receptor interactions.
accept: affinity is ability to bind the receptor while intrinsic activity is ability to activate it
binding strength versus capacity to elicit a response

questions.q: What are the affinity and intrinsic activity (IA) values of a pure competitive receptor antagonist?
options: Zero affinity and maximum intrinsic activity (IA = 1)
High affinity and zero intrinsic activity (IA = 0)
Zero affinity and zero intrinsic activity (IA = 0)
High affinity and negative intrinsic activity (IA = -1)
questions.explain: A neutral antagonist binds to the receptor (affinity > 0) without activating it (IA = 0), thereby preventing endogenous or exogenous agonists from binding.

open.q: State the affinity and intrinsic activity of a pure receptor antagonist.
accept: positive affinity and zero intrinsic activity

questions.q: What is a partial agonist, such as buprenorphine or pindolol?
options: A drug that binds to only half the organs in the body
A drug with a greater maximal response than a full agonist
A high-affinity ligand with submaximal efficacy that can oppose a full agonist
A drug that irreversibly destroys receptor proteins
questions.explain: A partial agonist cannot elicit 100% maximal tissue response even at full receptor occupancy, and when co-administered with a full agonist, it competes for receptors and lowers the net response.

open.q: Define a partial agonist and explain why it can act as an antagonist in the presence of a full agonist.
accept: has affinity but submaximal intrinsic activity so it competes with a full agonist and reduces maximal response
binds receptor with partial efficacy and blocks full agonist binding

questions.q: How does an inverse agonist (such as beta-carbolines at GABA-A receptors) differ pharmacologically from a neutral competitive antagonist?
options: An inverse agonist increases basal receptor activity
It binds only to intracellular DNA
It stabilises inactive receptors and lowers constitutive activity
questions.explain: In receptor systems with constitutive (ligand-independent) activity, a neutral antagonist blocks agonists without changing basal tone, whereas an inverse agonist actively suppresses basal signaling.

open.q: Explain how an inverse agonist alters receptor activity compared with a neutral antagonist.
accept: reduces constitutive basal receptor activity below baseline
stabilizes inactive state and lowers resting receptor tone

questions.q: How does the presence of a reversible competitive antagonist (such as atropine against acetylcholine) alter the log dose-response curve of an agonist?
options: Shifts the curve right (higher EC50) without lowering Emax
questions.explain: Because reversible competitive inhibition is surmountable by increasing agonist concentration, a higher agonist dose is needed for 50% effect (higher EC50), but the same Emax can still be achieved.

open.q: Describe the effect of a reversible competitive antagonist on the EC50 and Emax of an agonist's log dose-response curve.
accept: increases EC50 (rightward parallel shift) with no change in Emax
shifts curve to the right while preserving maximal efficacy

questions.q: How does a non-competitive or irreversible antagonist (such as phenoxybenzamine at alpha-adrenoceptors) affect the agonist log dose-response curve when no spare receptors exist?
options: Shifts the curve left and raises Emax
Lowers Emax because excess agonist cannot overcome the block
questions.explain: Irreversible or allosteric non-competitive antagonists remove functional receptors from the pool, making the block insurmountable and lowering Emax.

open.q: How does a non-competitive antagonist alter the maximal response (Emax) of an agonist on a dose-response curve?

questions.q: What is the concept of 'spare receptors' (receptor reserve)?
options: A maximal response occurs despite occupancy of only some receptors
Receptors found only in fetal life
questions.explain: When spare receptors exist (e.g., myocardial beta-1 receptors), EC50 is much lower than the dissociation constant Kd, and low doses of an irreversible antagonist initially shift the curve right before Emax falls.

open.q: Define spare receptors (receptor reserve).
accept: maximal response occurs when only a fraction of receptors is occupied
Emax is achieved without 100% receptor occupancy

questions.q: What does the EC50 (or ED50) on a graded dose-response curve measure?
questions.explain: Potency refers to the amount of drug required to produce an effect of given intensity; a lower EC50 indicates a more potent drug.

open.q: Which pharmacological property of a drug is measured by its EC50 (or ED50) on a graded dose-response curve?

questions.q: Drug A achieves a maximal analgesic effect at a dose of 10 mg (ED50 = 2 mg), whereas Drug B achieves the exact same maximal analgesic effect at a dose of 100 mg (ED50 = 20 mg). Which comparison is correct?
options: Drug A is ten times more potent than Drug B, and both have equal efficacy
Drug A has ten times greater efficacy than Drug B
Drug B is safer and has a wider therapeutic index than Drug A
Drug B is a partial agonist compared to Drug A
questions.explain: Potency depends on the dose needed for a given effect (Drug A requires one-tenth the dose), while clinical efficacy (Emax) is the ceiling response achieved, which is identical for both.

open.q: Compare the potency and efficacy of Drug A (ED50 = 2 mg, Emax = 100%) and Drug B (ED50 = 20 mg, Emax = 100%).
accept: Drug A is 10 times more potent and both have equal efficacy
A has higher potency and same efficacy

questions.q: How is the Therapeutic Index (TI) calculated from quantal population dose-response curves?
questions.explain: TI = TD50 / ED50 (or LD50 / ED50 in animal studies), comparing the median toxic dose to the median effective dose; a larger TI indicates a wider margin of safety.

open.q: State the formula for calculating the Therapeutic Index (TI) from quantal dose-response data.

questions.q: Why is the Certain Safety Factor (LD1 / ED99) sometimes preferred over the standard Therapeutic Index (LD50 / ED50) when evaluating drug safety?
options: It removes the need for plasma measurements
LD1/ED99 accounts for overlap between effective and lethal dose ranges
It measures potency rather than toxicity
questions.explain: Two drugs can share the same LD50/ED50 ratio, yet if the toxicity curve has a shallow slope, an ED99 dose might overlap with the lethal range; LD1/ED99 detects this overlap.

open.q: State the formula for the Certain Safety Factor and explain why it is clinically more informative than the standard Therapeutic Index.
accept: LD1 divided by ED99 because it accounts for the slopes of the effective and lethal dose-response curves
TD1/ED99 detects overlap between high therapeutic doses and low toxic doses

questions.q: Which type of drug antagonism occurs when two agonists act on DIFFERENT receptors to produce opposing physiological effects (such as adrenaline vs histamine on bronchial smooth muscle)?
questions.explain: In physiological antagonism, adrenaline stimulates beta-2 receptors (bronchodilation) while histamine stimulates H1 receptors (bronchoconstriction), counteracting each other via separate receptors.

open.q: Name the type of antagonism in which two drugs act at different receptors to produce opposing physiological actions.

questions.q: Which type of antagonism occurs when positively charged protamine sulfate binds directly to negatively charged heparin in plasma to neutralize its anticoagulant activity?
questions.explain: Chemical antagonism involves direct ionic or covalent interaction between two substances in solution without any receptor involvement (also seen with chelating agents and antacids).

open.q: Identify the type of antagonism exemplified by protamine sulfate neutralizing heparin directly in the bloodstream.

questions.q: What is 'tachyphylaxis'?
options: Rapid tolerance after closely spaced doses
Rapid renal drug clearance in children
questions.explain: Tachyphylaxis is rapid desensitization occurring over minutes to hours (e.g., repeated ephedrine or tyramine doses depleting noradrenaline stores, or continuous nitroglycerin infusion depleting sulfhydryl groups).

open.q: Define tachyphylaxis and give one classic drug example.
accept: rapid acute tolerance developing after a few doses such as ephedrine or nitrates
sudden loss of drug responsiveness on repeated administration over a short time

questions.q: Which molecular sequence mediates homologous desensitization and internalization of activated G-protein-coupled receptors?
options: GRK phosphorylation followed by beta-arrestin binding and endocytosis
cGMP binding to the receptor exterior
questions.explain: GRKs phosphorylate the intracellular C-terminal tail of persistently stimulated GPCRs, recruiting beta-arrestin which sterically uncouples the G-protein and promotes clathrin-mediated endocytosis.

open.q: Name the two key protein families that mediate homologous desensitization and endocytosis of overstimulated GPCRs.

questions.q: What happens to myocardial beta-1 adrenoceptor density during prolonged therapy with a beta-blocker like propranolol, and why must the drug NOT be stopped abruptly?
options: Receptor density stays fixed after withdrawal
Upregulation may cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension or ischaemia
questions.explain: Chronic receptor blockade increases surface receptor synthesis/externalization (upregulation/supersensitivity); sudden cessation precipitates rebound hypertension, tachycardia, and ischaemia.

open.q: Explain why abrupt discontinuation of chronic beta-blocker therapy can precipitate rebound tachycardia or angina.
accept: beta-receptor upregulation causing supersensitivity to endogenous catecholamines
upregulation of adrenoceptors during chronic blockade

questions.q: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with pinpoint pupils, a respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min, and coma after an opioid overdose. Intravenous naloxone rapidly restores his breathing. How does naloxone act?
options: Chemical chelation of morphine in plasma
Physiological stimulation of medullary beta-2 receptors
questions.explain: Naloxone is a pure competitive antagonist at mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors with high affinity and zero intrinsic activity, displacing opioid agonists from receptors.

open.q: State the receptor mechanism by which naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression.

questions.q: A patient with phaeochromocytoma is prepared for surgery using phenoxybenzamine, which forms a covalent bond with alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenoceptors. Why does the alpha-blockade persist for several days even after the drug is cleared from plasma?
options: Irreversible blockade requires synthesis of new α-adrenoceptors
questions.explain: Phenoxybenzamine is a haloalkylamine that alkylates alpha-adrenoceptors irreversibly; restoration of sympathetic vasoconstriction depends on de novo receptor protein turnover.

open.q: Explain why the pharmacological action of phenoxybenzamine lasts for days despite its short plasma half-life.
accept: irreversible covalent binding requiring new receptor synthesis

questions.q: How do benzodiazepines such as diazepam act as positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) at the GABA-A receptor?
options: They open GABA-A channels without GABA
Positive allosteric modulation increases GABA affinity and channel-opening frequency
questions.explain: Benzodiazepines bind at the interface between alpha and gamma subunits of GABA-A receptors (an allosteric site separate from the GABA binding site) and require endogenous GABA to increase Cl- channel opening frequency.

open.q: Explain the allosteric mechanism of benzodiazepines at the GABA-A receptor.
accept: positive allosteric modulators that increase the frequency of chloride channel opening in the presence of GABA
bind an allosteric site to enhance GABA affinity and channel opening frequency

questions.q: Which antianginal drug acts as an arterial and venous vasodilator by opening ATP-sensitive K+ channels and simultaneously donating nitric oxide?
questions.explain: Nicorandil has a dual mechanism: its nicotinamide moiety opens sarcolemmal K_ATP channels (hyperpolarizing vascular smooth muscle) and its nitrate group activates soluble guanylyl cyclase.

open.q: Name the antianginal agent that acts both as a K_ATP channel opener and a nitric oxide donor.

questions.q: Which enzyme is inhibited by captopril, enalapril, and lisinopril?
questions.explain: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, preventing conversion of angiotensin I to vasoconstrictor angiotensin II and inhibiting the breakdown of vasodilator bradykinin.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by drugs such as captopril and enalapril.

questions.q: How does omeprazole suppress gastric acid secretion?
options: Competitive blockade of histamine H2 receptors
Irreversible covalent inhibition of the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase proton pump
Neutralization of acid inside the duodenal bulb
questions.explain: Omeprazole is concentrated in the acidic parietal canaliculus, converted to an active sulfenamide, and forms disulfide bonds with cysteine residues on H+/K+-ATPase.

open.q: Identify the specific membrane pump irreversibly inhibited by omeprazole in gastric parietal cells.

questions.q: Which class of antihypertensive and antianginal drugs blocks L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and myocardium?
questions.explain: Calcium channel blockers bind the alpha-1 subunit of L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, reducing Ca2+ influx, peripheral vascular resistance, and (for verapamil/diltiazem) SA/AV nodal conduction.

open.q: Which specific subtype of calcium channel is blocked by nifedipine, amlodipine, verapamil, and diltiazem?

questions.q: Which second messenger activates Protein Kinase A (PKA) by binding to its regulatory subunits and releasing active catalytic subunits?
questions.explain: Four molecules of cAMP bind to the two regulatory subunits of inactive PKA holoenzyme, releasing two active catalytic subunits that phosphorylate target serine/threonine residues.

open.q: Name the second messenger that directly activates protein kinase A (PKA).

questions.q: Which second messenger directly activates Protein Kinase C (PKC) in cooperation with intracellular calcium and phosphatidylserine?
questions.explain: Membrane-bound diacylglycerol (DAG), generated by phospholipase C cleavage of PIP2, recruits and activates protein kinase C at the inner plasma membrane leaflet.

open.q: Name the lipid second messenger generated from PIP2 that activates protein kinase C.

questions.q: How is the signal of an activated G-alpha-GTP subunit terminated physiologically?
options: G-alpha hydrolyses GTP to GDP, a process accelerated by RGS proteins
The GPCR is cleaved by thrombin
Adenylyl cyclase phosphorylates GDP to GTP
questions.explain: G-alpha possesses intrinsic GTPase activity (enhanced by Regulators of G-protein Signaling, RGS) that hydrolyzes GTP to GDP, allowing G-alpha-GDP to reassociate with G-beta-gamma.

open.q: Explain how G-protein signaling is switched off after agonist activation.
accept: intrinsic GTPase activity of G-alpha hydrolyzes GTP to GDP
hydrolysis of GTP to GDP allowing reassociation of alpha and beta-gamma subunits

questions.q: Which intracellular calcium-binding protein mediates smooth muscle contraction by activating myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) once cytosolic Ca2+ rises?
questions.explain: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; instead, four Ca2+ ions bind calmodulin, and the Ca2+-calmodulin complex activates MLCK to phosphorylate myosin light chains and trigger contraction.

open.q: Name the intracellular calcium-binding protein that activates myosin light-chain kinase in vascular and bronchial smooth muscle.

questions.q: What is a 'biased agonist' (functional selectivity) at a G-protein-coupled receptor?
options: A drug effective only in men
A drug that binds only mutant cancer receptors
A drug equally potent at all receptors
A ligand that preferentially activates one signalling pathway
questions.explain: Biased agonists selectively engage specific intracellular effectors (such as G-protein signaling without beta-arrestin recruitment), offering the potential for therapeutic efficacy with fewer adverse effects.

open.q: Define biased agonism (functional selectivity) at a G-protein-coupled receptor.
accept: selective activation of one downstream signaling pathway over another by the same receptor
preferential signaling through G-protein versus beta-arrestin

questions.q: What does a quantal dose-response curve measure across a population of subjects?
options: Proportion of a population showing an all-or-none response at each dose
Continuous heart-rate increase in one atrium
questions.explain: Unlike graded dose-response curves (which measure continuous intensity in one biological system), quantal curves plot the frequency of a defined all-or-none endpoint (e.g., sleep, seizure prevention, death) in a population.

open.q: Distinguish a quantal dose-response curve from a graded dose-response curve.
accept: quantal measures all-or-none responses across a population while graded measures continuous response magnitude in a single system
population frequency of binary endpoint versus continuous intensity

questions.q: Why are drug dose-response relationships conventionally plotted with the logarithm of the drug concentration on the horizontal axis?
options: It compresses the concentration range and produces a sigmoid curve
It removes the need to measure efficacy
Receptors bind only at logarithmic intervals
questions.explain: A semilogarithmic plot allows comparison of drugs differing in potency by orders of magnitude and yields a nearly linear central segment between 20% and 80% of Emax.

open.q: State two advantages of plotting drug concentration on a logarithmic scale in dose-response graphs.
accept: compresses wide dose ranges and produces a sigmoid curve with a linear middle section
facilitates potency comparison and linearizes the 20 to 80 percent response range

questions.q: Which antiplatelet drug irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor after hepatic bioactivation by CYP2C19?
questions.explain: Clopidogrel is a thienopyridine prodrug converted by CYP2C19 into an active metabolite that forms a disulfide bridge to irreversibly inhibit platelet P2Y12 receptors.

open.q: Name the thienopyridine antiplatelet prodrug that irreversibly inhibits platelet P2Y12 ADP receptors.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency unit with profuse salivation, lacrimation, bronchospasm, miosis, and muscle fasciculations after accidental exposure to malathion insecticide. How does malathion produce these effects?
options: Blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels at sympathetic ganglia
Competitive antagonism of muscarinic M3 receptors
Irreversible phosphorylation and inactivation of acetylcholinesterase
questions.explain: Organophosphate insecticides (malathion, parathion) phosphorylate the serine hydroxyl group at the active site of acetylcholinesterase; if untreated, 'aging' makes the inhibition permanent.

open.q: State the enzyme mechanism by which organophosphate insecticides such as malathion cause cholinergic crisis.
accept: irreversible phosphorylation and inhibition of acetylcholinesterase

questions.q: A 19-year-old student with severe acute asthma receives nebulized salbutamol (a beta-2 agonist) alongside intravenous hydrocortisone. Why does hydrocortisone restore responsiveness to salbutamol in a patient who had become refractory to beta-2 agonists?
options: Glucocorticoids upregulate β2 receptors and reverse desensitisation
It acts as an alveolar osmotic diuretic
questions.explain: Glucocorticoids increase beta-2 adrenoceptor gene transcription and prevent receptor downregulation, restoring bronchodilator sensitivity in status asthmaticus.

open.q: Explain the receptor-level permissive mechanism by which corticosteroids restore bronchodilator responsiveness to beta-2 agonists in severe asthma.
accept: upregulation of beta-2 adrenoceptor synthesis and reversal of desensitization

questions.q: What is 'synergism' (supra-additive drug interaction) between two drugs such as sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim?
options: The combined effect equals the simple arithmetic sum of their individual effects
The combined effect is substantially greater than the sum of their individual effects alone
One drug completely abolishes the therapeutic action of the other
Both drugs bind to plasma albumin without exerting any biological action
questions.explain: In synergism (potentiation), sequential blockade of tetrahydrofolate synthesis by sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim turns two bacteriostatic agents into a bactericidal combination.

open.q: Define pharmacological synergism.
accept: combined effect of two drugs is greater than the sum of their individual effects

questions.q: What is 'potentiation' in pharmacology, as illustrated by combining carbidopa with levodopa?
options: Two active drugs produce the same effect at one receptor
A drug loses effect after repeated dosing
Carbidopa enhances levodopa by inhibiting peripheral metabolism
Two drugs precipitate in an infusion bag
questions.explain: Carbidopa has no antiparkinsonian action on its own, but by inhibiting peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, it markedly increases the CNS delivery and efficacy of levodopa.

open.q: Define potentiation and give one clinical drug combination example.
accept: enhancement of an active drug's effect by a second compound with no intrinsic activity of its own such as levodopa plus carbidopa
inactive drug boosting the action of an active drug e.g. amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid

questions.q: Which intracellular receptor subtype is targeted by atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)?
questions.explain: NPR-A and NPR-B are single-transmembrane receptors possessing intrinsic intracellular guanylyl cyclase domains that generate cGMP directly upon ANP/BNP binding.

open.q: Identify the receptor signaling mechanism activated by atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP).

questions.q: Which enzyme is inhibited by allopurinol and febuxostat in the treatment of chronic gout?
questions.explain: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid; inhibiting it lowers serum urate levels.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by allopurinol to reduce uric acid production.

questions.q: How do statins such as atorvastatin and rosuvastatin lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis?
questions.explain: Statins are structural analogues of HMG-CoA that competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, depleting hepatocyte cholesterol and upregulating hepatic LDL receptors.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis inhibited by statins.

questions.q: Why does cardiac beta-1 adrenoceptor activation increase heart rate (positive chronotropy) and contractility (positive inotropy)?
options: Stimulating Gi and closing L-type Ca2+ channels
Opening GABA-gated chloride channels in the SA node
Activating Gs–cAMP–PKA to increase calcium entry and pacemaker rate
questions.explain: Gs-cAMP-PKA signaling enhances Ca2+ influx through L-type channels, accelerates SERCA Ca2+ reuptake via phospholamban phosphorylation, and speeds diastolic depolarization in the SA node.

open.q: Outline the G-protein and second messenger pathway mediating positive inotropy and chronotropy after beta-1 adrenoceptor stimulation.
accept: Gs activation stimulates adenylyl cyclase raising cAMP and activating PKA

questions.q: Why does bronchial beta-2 adrenoceptor stimulation cause smooth muscle relaxation (bronchodilation) via the exact same Gs-cAMP-PKA pathway that causes contraction in cardiac muscle?
options: Bronchial smooth muscle lacks actin and myosin
PKA depletes ATP in airway muscle
PKA inhibits myosin light-chain kinase, promoting relaxation
questions.explain: Tissue-specific intracellular substrates determine the physiological outcome: in smooth muscle, PKA inhibits MLCK and promotes Ca2+ sequestration, whereas in myocardium PKA enhances Ca2+ cycling.

open.q: Explain how elevation of cAMP and PKA activation causes relaxation in bronchial smooth muscle.
accept: PKA phosphorylates and inhibits myosin light-chain kinase
inactivation of MLCK and lowering of intracellular Ca2+

questions.q: What is 'heterologous desensitization' of receptors?
options: One receptor pathway dampens another through shared signalling components
Only the stimulated receptor can desensitise
questions.explain: In heterologous desensitization, second-messenger kinases (PKA or PKC) activated by one receptor phosphorylate other nearby receptors or signaling effectors, dampening responses across multiple receptor classes.

open.q: Distinguish heterologous receptor desensitization from homologous receptor desensitization.
accept: heterologous reduces responsiveness of multiple receptor types sharing downstream pathways whereas homologous affects only the stimulated receptor
cross-desensitization of different receptors versus self-desensitization of one receptor

questions.q: Which antidepressant class acts by inhibiting the mitochondrial enzyme that oxidatively deaminates noradrenaline, serotonin, and dopamine in presynaptic nerve terminals?
questions.explain: MAOIs inhibit mitochondrial monoamine oxidase (MAO-A and MAO-B), increasing intraneuronal stores of monoamine neurotransmitters available for synaptic release.

open.q: Name the class of antidepressants that prevents intraneuronal breakdown of monoamines by inhibiting mitochondrial monoamine oxidase.

questions.q: How does activated charcoal prevent systemic toxicity in acute oral drug poisoning?
options: Chemical oxidation of toxins to carbon dioxide and water
Adsorption of drug molecules onto a porous GI surface
questions.explain: Activated charcoal possesses an enormous microporous surface area that physically adsorbs many organic toxins in the gut lumen, preventing their mucosal absorption.

open.q: State the physical mechanism by which activated charcoal reduces gastrointestinal absorption of ingested poisons.

questions.q: Which pharmacokinetic interaction exemplifies 'pharmacokinetic antagonism', where one drug reduces the plasma concentration of another drug at its site of action?
options: Phenobarbital induces hepatic CYP enzymes, increasing warfarin metabolism
questions.explain: Pharmacokinetic antagonism occurs when the antagonist reduces absorption, increases metabolism, or accelerates excretion of the active drug, lowering its effective concentration at the target receptor.

open.q: Define pharmacokinetic antagonism and give one example.
accept: one drug reduces the concentration of another drug at its site of action by altering absorption metabolism or excretion such as rifampicin reducing warfarin levels
reduction of active drug concentration via altered ADME

questions.q: Which antibiotic inhibits bacterial folate synthesis by competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase through structural mimicry of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)?
questions.explain: Sulfonamides are structural analogues of PABA that competitively inhibit bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, whereas trimethoprim inhibits the subsequent enzyme, dihydrofolate reductase.

open.q: Name the bacterial enzyme competitively inhibited by sulfonamides via structural mimicry of PABA.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with heart failure taking digoxin is started on furosemide and develops ventricular arrhythmias and yellow-green visual halos. How does furosemide-induced hypokalaemia precipitate digoxin toxicity at the molecular target?
options: Low K+ accelerates digoxin conversion to a toxic alkaloid
K+ competes with digoxin at Na+/K+-ATPase; hypokalaemia increases digoxin binding
Hypokalaemia makes digoxin a calcium-channel agonist
Low K+ permanently opens cardiac KATP channels
questions.explain: Extracellular K+ and digoxin compete for the same extracellular binding site on the alpha subunit of Na+/K+-ATPase; hypokalaemia enhances digoxin binding and precipitates toxicity.

open.q: Explain at the receptor/enzyme level why hypokalaemia predisposes patients to digoxin toxicity.
accept: potassium competes with digoxin for binding to Na+/K+-ATPase so low K+ increases digoxin binding
reduced competition by K+ at the sodium-potassium pump
